news.title: Newsom Says He Won’t Run for President in 2028 If Kamala Harris Does
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom said on Sept. 14 that he would not run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris decides to make another presidential bid.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom, a Democrat, told CNN anchor Jake Tapper in an interview. “I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

Newsom said that running against Harris, who became the Democratic presidential candidate during the 2024 election after then-President Joe Biden withdrew his bid, would be an electoral gift for their political opponents and “waste everyone’s time.”

“First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good,” the governor said.

When asked about the fact that Harris had launched presidential bids in 2019 and 2024, while Newsom had never run for president, Newsom said that could be an “approach to the campaign,” but that he would be competing for the same voters who supported Harris.

“That’s objectively true. But I know what that means. I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the Venn diagram on that is just pure crossover. I wouldn’t do that to people,” he said.

Harris, who was vice president at the time, lost the 2024 election to Republican Donald Trump, who returned to the White House for a second term. She previously launched a presidential bid for the 2020 election but dropped out two months before the primary voting began.

Newsom said he was not ready to run for president in 2024.

“If I did, I would have gotten crushed because I didn’t have a why. You don’t have a big enough why, then you don’t belong there,” the governor said.

Harris has hinted that she may run for president again in 2028. During the National Action Network’s annual convention in New York City in April, Harris said that she was “thinking about” another presidential run.

Harris previously served as California’s attorney general before representing the state in the U.S. Senate from 2017 to 2021.

Newsom, who was elected governor in 2018 and won reelection in 2022, is term-limited and cannot seek a third consecutive term. He will leave office in January 2027.
news.author: Aldgra Fredly

news.title: Stephen Colbert Ignores Donald Trump During Emmys Speech
news.text: The Late Show with Stephen Colbert ended its 11-year run with an Emmy win Monday night—and in a speech that could have become a political final word, Colbert chose to make it a thank-you. “I want to say to the audience, thank you so much for watching,” Colbert said as he ended his nearly two-minute-long speech. “We hope you enjoyed the show. We had a great time doing it for you.” Colbert did not mention Donald Trump in his Emmy speech, despite the president being a frequent target of his political comedy throughout the show's run. Trump repeatedly criticized Colbert and The Late Show. After CBS announced the cancellation in 2025, Trump celebrated the decision on Truth Social, writing, “I hear Jimmy Kimmel is next. Has even less talent than Colbert!” The Late Show aired for the final time in May 2026. Colbert dedicated much of Monday night's acceptance speech to the more than 200 people who made the show possible, calling late night a “fantastic incubator” for young people learning to work under pressure and collaborate. “They are all tech-avail,” Colbert joked, urging the industry to hire his former colleagues. “Hire them, they will make your show better, and they will make your day easier.” Colbert also noted that his writing team, which won the show’s first Emmy for variety series writing last weekend, was responsible for writing Monday night’s Emmy jokes. He thanked the many guests he had interviewed before turning to his wife, Evelyn “Evie” McGee Colbert, whom he called his favorite guest. He closed by thanking the audience for watching, saying he and his team had “a great time” making the show for them. “That’s it. Thank you. We’ll catch you all on the flip,” he said. Colbert won the Emmy in a field that included The Daily Show, Jimmy Kimmel Live!, Last Week Tonight With John Oliver and Saturday Night Live. The category was also different this year. The Television Academy combined the former Outstanding Talk Series and Outstanding Scripted Variety Series categories into a single Outstanding Variety Series award and reclassified it as an “area award.” Instead of choosing one winner, voters evaluated each nominee individually with a yes-or-no vote. Any show that received at least 90 percent “yes” votes could win, meaning multiple shows could take home the Emmy in the same year. Two weeks ago, Colbert endorsed fellow nominee Jimmy Kimmel in an Instagram video saying, “I think we can all agree that Jimmy Kimmel deserves an Emmy.” Kimmel applauded as Colbert delivered his speech Monday night. The show ran for 11 seasons with Colbert at the helm, following David Letterman’s 22-year run as host and bringing the Late Show franchise’s total run on CBS to 33 years. Its final episode aired in May 2026 and drew 6.74 million viewers, making it the most-watched weeknight episode in the show’s history, according to CBS data. The cancellation came just days after Colbert criticized CBS parent company Paramount for its $16 million settlement of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump over a 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Colbert denounced the deal as a “big fat bribe” while Paramount was seeking approval for its merger with Skydance Media. CBS said it was “purely a financial decision against a challenging backdrop in late night,” stressing that it was not “related in any way to the show’s performance, content or other matters happening at Paramount.” Colbert is currently working on The Lord of the Rings: Shadow of the Past with his son, Peter McGee, according to IMDbPro. He's also listed as executive producer on The Chronicles of Amber and Hello, Nancy. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: After 11 seasons, the late-night host takes home an Emmy as he delivers a heartfelt farewell to his audience and crew.

news.title: James Talarico Polls Compared to Beto O'Rourke When He Almost Beat Ted Cruz
news.text: James Talarico is polling better in his Senate race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton than Beto O'Rourke was at this point in the 2018 campaign, when he almost beat Senator Ted Cruz. Democrats have been hoping to win in Texas for years and have come up short in every race, but this year, ratings have the Senate race as a toss-up. If Talarico wins, it'll be the first time a Democrat has won a Senate race in Texas in nearly 40 years, and Cruz has warned that if Democrats win Texas, they can dominate the country for a century. James Talarico's Chances of Beating Ken Paxton A new poll from SoCal Strategies found Talarico leading Paxton with 50 percent of the vote to Paxton's 45 percent. It’s a flip from June, when the same pollster found Paxton leading the race. Talarico’s seen major increases in support among Hispanic voters, going from 10 percent in June to 38 percent in the recent poll, and his support among independent voters went from 10 percent to 45 percent. Twelve percent of Republicans also plan to vote for the Democratic candidate. "Much like the last poll, Republicans are less decided than Democrats. While six percent of respondents who said they backed Trump in 2024 are currently undecided in the Senate race, the same can only be said of one percent of those who say they voted for [Vice President Kamala] Harris," the survey report said. "To have a chance, Paxton will need to win nearly all of these voters and peel back a substantial portion of the 12% of Republicans who say they would vote for Talarico if the election were held today." Talarico's odds of winning the election have also flipped on market predictor websites. Polymarket gives Talarico a 53 percent chance of winning, a shift from the end of July when Paxton was expected to win with 56 percent odds. Kalshi gives Talarico similar odds, at 52 percent, a shift from a few days ago when Paxton was expected to win by a similar margin. Beto O'Rourke's Chances of Beating Ted Cruz At This Point in 2018 Campaign At this point in the 2018 campaign, Cruz was leading O'Rourke by about 3 points, according to a Real Clear Politics average of polls. Cruz would go on to beat O'Rourke by 2 points in the election. At the time, Cruz praised O'Rourke for the campaign that he won and admitted that it was a close race. Now, Cruz is warning that Democrats could win. On a recent podcast, Cruz said Republicans "could lose Texas," and in July, he said he thinks Talarico has a “real chance.” “I think this is a real race. I think it’s going to be close. I think we’re going to win, I think we’re going to keep Texas red, but the polling right now shows this is a 1- or 2-point race,” Cruz told Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who was guest hosting Sean Hannity’s radio show. Cruz also recently told Sean Spicer, who served as press secretary to President Donald Trump during his first term, that he’s “really worried” about the Senate. He included Texas on the list of “very competitive” Senate races and said it could be a “really rough election” for Republicans. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Senator Ted Cruz has warned that Texas is a competitive race and it's possible Republicans could lose.

news.title: Is America Ready for a Gay President?
news.text:
During an appearance on NBC's Meet the Press, host Kristen Welker asked Buttigieg about his blatantly obvious presidential ambitions. She asked him directly whether America was truly ready to elect a gay president, bringing up what Kamala Harris’s ghostwriter wrote in her memoir.

“I do want to talk a bit about your political future, Mr. Secretary,” Welker began. “Former Vice President Kamala Harris wrote in her book about the 2024 election that you came close to being her running mate. Let me remind people of this passage. She writes of the eight names on the list for vetting. ‘I might as well say that Pete Buttigieg was my first choice. He would have been an ideal partner if I were a straight white man. But knowing what was at stake, it was too big of a risk.’ She was essentially saying that she didn’t think America was ready for a gay vice president with a black woman at the top of the ticket. Let me ask you today, do you think America is ready for a gay president?”

As you might expect, Buttigieg didn't hedge.

"I wouldn't have run for president in the first place if I didn't believe that," he insisted. "Of course."

And then he kept talking.

"My experience in South Bend, Indiana, getting re-elected with 80% of the vote after coming out, and my experience right now traveling the country shows me that what's really on people's minds isn't about you, your identity as a candidate," he continued. "It's about them. It's about their lives."

Welker then asked him whether he'd commit to running in 2028, even though it is pretty obvious he’s planning to run. "I don't think now is the time to even be talking about that," he said. "I think by my count, we've been to 35 states since I left the cabinet."

He happened to be in New Mexico at the time, a state that falls on the early presidential primary calendar — some coincidence.

Buttigieg clearly understands what Kamala's calculus proved. A gay identity is an asset inside today's Democrat base. Why? Because Democrats thrive on identity politics, and every national ticket for twenty years has carried some kind of "historic first" as a gimmick. In 2008, it was that Barack Obama would have been the first black man elected president. In 2016, Hillary Clinton would have been the first woman elected president. In 2020, Kamala became the first female vice president. In 2024, she would have been the first female president.

At this rate, every Democrat ticket going forward will feature a woman or a minority somewhere on it.

So the identity-politics box has been checked plenty of times already. The open question is whether America will check the one Buttigieg is banking on: an openly gay man in the Oval Office.

I'm not sold that it will. Yes, America's views on same-sex marriage and homosexuality have shifted dramatically over the last 30 years, and Buttigieg himself doesn't scare anyone. He was a lousy transportation secretary, but he comes across as a normal guy. The trouble starts once you get past the B in LGBTQ+ and into the T and the Q and whatever the plus is, and recent polling shows Americans swinging against mutilation of children, the unfairness of letting biological men compete in women's sports, and all that nonsense about there being more than two genders.

Buttigieg didn't build that brand, but guess what? He's stuck carrying it. And until voters stop associating the TQ+ with the LGB, a gay president isn't happening, no matter how many states he visits or how normal he seems.
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: Gavin Newsom reveals he won’t run for president in 2028 if a certain other Democrat does
news.text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has revealed that he won’t run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris does. 

Newsom is considered a top potential Democratic candidate in the next presidential election, which is a little more than two years away. While the governor is still weighing a potential run, he told CNN’s Jake Tapper in a new interview that he wouldn’t throw his hat in the ring if Harris was in the race. 

“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom said while fly fishing in Montana with Tapper as part of a series where the news anchor chats with politicians in some of their favorite places. “Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time.”

When Tapper asked Newsom to explain, the governor suggested that pitting two California Democrats against each other would force their shared base to choose between them, handing an advantage to the other candidates. 

“Electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it — mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good,” Newsom said. 

The governor endorsed Harris when former President Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 presidential election, writing on X, “With our democracy at stake and our future on the line, no one is better to prosecute the case against Donald Trump’s dark vision and guide our country in a healthier direction than [Harris].” 

Newsom, who has gained popularity during Donald Trump’s second term for mocking the president online, also has five other people to consider when deciding to run in 2028 — his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, and their four kids. 

“I know what matters in life,” Newsom told Tapper in a clip of their interview, which will air in full Tuesday. “I’ve got four kids. It’s the only thing that matters to me. They gotta be on board.”

When Politico’s Jonathan Martin asked Newsom in a March interview whether his kids would want him to run for president, the governor said, “It depends on the day of the week.”

Newsom then told a story of his teenage son asking him about running in 2028.

When Newsom denied that he had decided on a presidential bid, his son said, “Good.” The California governor then asked him what he meant by that, and his son replied, “We’re too young and you need to spend more time with us.”

Other names widely floated as potential Democratic candidates in 2028 are progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Biden’s Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who ran for president in 2020. 

In a Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll of likely voters released earlier this month, Harris received 17 percent of support for the Democratic nomination and Newsom received 14 percent. 

Buttigieg closely trailed Harris with 16 percent support and Ocasio-Cortez tied Newsom at 14 percent. 

On the GOP side, Vice President JD Vance received 44 percent support for the Republican nomination and Secretary of State Marco Rubio received 21 percent.
news.summary: California governor’s name has been thrown out as a potential Democratic candidate in the 2028 presidential election — as have AOC, Pete Buttigieg and Kamala Harris
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Stephen Colbert’s Canceled ‘Late Show’ Won Its Emmy, And He Used It To Pitch His Staff: ‘Hire Them’
news.text:
“The Late Show” may be over, but it’s still a winner.

Stephen Colbert’s late-night talk show picked up one of its biggest honors Monday night, winning Outstanding Variety Series for its final season. It came out on top over fellow nominees “Saturday Night Live,” “The Daily Show,” “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver” and “Jimmy Kimmel Live!”

Colbert started his acceptance speech off by plugging his old “The Late Show” writers, some of whom worked on this year’s Emmy Awards.

“I want you to know I got some great news,” the former host told the Emmys audience. “They are all tech avail. Hire them. They will make your show better, and they will make your day easier.”

Acknowledging his series’ run, Colbert also said: “Thank you so much on behalf of the over 200 people who threw themselves at this show for 11 years to try to do the best show they possibly could for you.”

“Thank you so much for watching,” he added. “We hope you enjoyed the show. We had a great time doing it for you. That’s it. Thank you. We’ll catch you all on the flipside.”

The “Late Show” win comes over a year after CBS controversially canceled the longtime show, bringing Colbert’s 11-season run to an end and closing out the program’s decades-long stint on the air.

But even before Monday’s primetime Emmys ceremony, “The Late Show” had already picked up five awards at last weekend’s Creative Arts Emmys, including Outstanding Writing and Directing for a Variety Series.

“The Late Show” wrapped up its run on May 21 with a star-studded finale that gave the longtime talk show a fitting sendoff. Music icon Paul McCartney, actors Ryan Reynolds, Paul Rudd and Bryan Cranston, and fellow late-night hosts Jimmy Fallon, Jimmy Kimmel, John Oliver and Seth Meyers all joined Colbert to bid his series farewell.

The finale also drew more than 6 million viewers, making it the show’s most-watched weeknight episode ever, according to Variety.

Colbert had been preparing for the goodbye episode since CBS announced the show’s abrupt cancellation, citing low ratings and financial difficulties. Still, the decision came shortly after the host criticized a $16 million settlement between Paramount Global, CBS’s parent company, and President Donald Trump over the editing of a “60 Minutes” interview with former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Colbert slammed the move on his now-canceled show, calling the settlement a “big, fat bribe” for the Trump administration to approve Paramount’s merger with Skydance Media.

“As someone who has always been a proud employee of this network, I am offended,” Colbert added. “I don’t know if anything — anything — will repair my trust in this company.”

Months after his final sign-off, a gray-bearded Colbert posted on Instagram in August to endorse his friend Kimmel for Best Variety Series at the Emmys. But Kimmel returned the favor, adding the tagline “I’m voting for Stephen” to one of his “For Your Consideration” billboards.
news.author: Njera Perkins

news.title: Stephen Colbert gets last laugh with ‘Late Show’ Emmy win after Trump attacks
news.text:
Stephen Colbert got the last laugh at the Emmys with a golden awards sendoff.

The former “Late Show” host victoriously took the stage Sept. 14 during the 78th Emmy Awards after his now-canceled late night CBS show won outstanding variety series, using the victory to advocate for his writing staff.

After pointing out that "if you like the comedy tonight, my old writers wrote it," Colbert said late-night shows are a "fantastic incubator for young people to come in" and learn how to work on a deadline.

"That is the future of our business that we have to look after," he said, adding that he has "great news" for the industry: His writers are now available to work. "Hire them. They will make your show better, and they will make your day easier."

Colbert also thanked those in the room who he has interviewed on his show but said his "favorite guest" is his wife, Evelyn McGee Colbert, whom he called the "only audience I really care about." 

The comedian also thanked her for being his "only audience" when he was taping his show at home during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Yours is the laugh that I want for the rest of my life," he said. "I love you."

Colbert concluded his speech by thanking his viewers: "Thank you so much for watching. We hope you enjoyed the show. We had a great time doing it for you. That's it. Thank you. We'll catch you all on the flip."

The win capped a fitting Emmy farewell for Colbert and “The Late Show,” which ended its 11-season run at New York City's famed Ed Sullivan Theater in May after CBS announced it was pulling the plug on the late-night institution in July 2025.

Vote: Who had the best look at the Emmys? Vote for your favorites in USA TODAY's Emmys Style Meter.

The cancellation turned into an instant political flashpoint. CBS maintained the decision was a financial reality in the changing late-night landscape. But it came amid intense scrutiny over parent company Paramount's relationship with President Donald Trump. 

Paramount had agreed to a $16 million settlement of Trump's lawsuit over a CBS “60 Minutes” interview with Kamala Harris, a deal Colbert blasted on his show as a “big fat bribe.”

Trump publicly celebrated news of Colbert's cancellation.

"I absolutely love that Colbert got fired. His talent was even less than his ratings," Trump wrote in a July 18 Truth Social post, before also ripping ABC's Jimmy Kimmel, another late-night host known to poke fun at Trump. "I hear Jimmy Kimmel is next. Has even less talent than Colbert."

Colbert, one of TV's most artful Trump critics, continued hammering the president through his final months on the air.

One hour after the May 21 TV conclusion of the his late-night series – at 1:52 a.m. – Trump poured water on the jubilant show finale from his Truth Social account. "Colbert is finally finished at CBS. Amazing that he lasted so long! No talent, no ratings, no life." 

But Colbert opted not to get political during his Emmys speech, ignoring Trump entirely in his remarks.

This was Colbert's second consecutive Emmy win for "The Late Show": In his 2025 acceptance speech, he thanked CBS for "giving us the privilege to be part of the late-night tradition, which I hope continues long after we're no longer doing this show."

“The Late Show” entered the Sept. 14 Emmys ceremony with considerable momentum after winning five Creative Arts Emmys the previous weekend, including awards for writing and directing. 

Colbert actually endorsed "Jimmy Kimmel Live" competitor Jimmy Kimmel to win the category in a sincere Instagram post on the last day of Emmy voting.

The win comes the same week that Page Six reported on Sept. 8 that this season Kimmel's late-night show will be its last. ABC denied the report, calling it "inaccurate" and saying that "any reports about the future of the show at this point are purely speculative." Days later, USA TODAY learned that Kimmel and ABC are currently in talks to renew his long-running show.

Contributing: Brendan Morrow, USA TODAY
